categories.title: Vascular Anatomy
categories.description: Master the anatomical structures and relationships of the vascular system

topics.title: Lower Extremity Arterial Anatomy
topics.quickSummary: The arterial system begins at the CFA and bifurcates into the SFA and profunda femoris, continuing to supply the lower extremity through the popliteal and tibial arteries.
clinicalPearls: The SFA is NOT a superficial vessel - it's a deep artery despite its name
The adductor hiatus is where the SFA becomes the popliteal artery - a key landmark
The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to the thigh, not the SFA

sections.title: Arterial Pathway
sections.content:
The common femoral artery (CFA) originates from the external iliac artery at the inguinal ligament. It then bifurcates into:

• Superficial Femoral Artery (SFA) - continues down the thigh
• Profunda Femoris (Deep Femoral) - supplies thigh muscles

sections.title: Key Anatomical Points
sections.content:
• CFA location: At the inguinal ligament
• SFA course: Travels through the adductor canal
• Adductor hiatus: Transition point where SFA becomes popliteal artery
• Popliteal trifurcation: Divides into anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries

sections.title: Clinical Significance
sections.content:
Understanding the arterial pathway is crucial for:
• Identifying stenosis locations
• Planning intervention approaches
• Recognizing collateral pathways
• Interpreting waveform changes

keyTakeaways: CFA bifurcates into SFA and profunda femoris
SFA becomes popliteal artery at adductor hiatus
Popliteal trifurcates into 3 tibial vessels
Profunda supplies thigh, not leg

topics.title: Lower Extremity Venous Anatomy
topics.quickSummary: The venous system has three components: deep veins (follow arteries), superficial veins (GSV, SSV), and perforating veins that connect them.
clinicalPearls: GSV is the longest vein in the body - runs from foot to groin
Remember: Deep veins are named same as arteries, superficial veins are not
The saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) is a common site for reflux
Perforators should only allow flow from superficial to deep

sections.title: Deep Venous System
sections.content:
The deep veins parallel the arterial system:

• Common Femoral Vein (CFV)
• Femoral Vein (FV) - formerly called superficial femoral vein
• Popliteal Vein
• Anterior Tibial Veins (paired)
• Posterior Tibial Veins (paired)
• Peroneal Veins (paired)

Note: Tibial veins are typically paired (2 veins accompanying each artery)

sections.title: Superficial Venous System
sections.content:
Superficial veins run in subcutaneous tissue:

• Great Saphenous Vein (GSV)
  - Longest vein in body
  - Runs medial leg from ankle to groin
  - Joins CFV at saphenofemoral junction (SFJ)

• Small Saphenous Vein (SSV)
  - Runs posterior calf
  - Joins popliteal vein at saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ)
  - Variable anatomy

sections.title: Perforating Veins
sections.content:
Connect superficial to deep systems:

• Allow one-way flow: superficial → deep
• Named perforators (exam favorites):
  - Cockett perforators (medial calf)
  - Boyd perforator (below knee)
  - Dodd perforator (thigh)
• Incompetent perforators contribute to venous insufficiency

keyTakeaways: Deep veins follow arteries and are named similarly
GSV is medial, SSV is posterior
Perforators connect superficial to deep (one-way valves)
Three venous systems work together for venous return

topics.title: Carotid & Cerebrovascular Anatomy
topics.quickSummary: The carotid system bifurcates into ICA (supplies brain, no extracranial branches) and ECA (supplies face, multiple branches).
clinicalPearls: ICA has NO extracranial branches - if you see branches, it's the ECA
ECA is typically smaller and anteromedial to ICA
Tap test: Temporal artery tap creates oscillations in ECA waveform
ICA waveform is low resistance (brain needs constant flow)

sections.title: Carotid Bifurcation
sections.content:
The common carotid artery (CCA) has NO branches until it bifurcates:

• CCA travels in neck with no branches
• Bifurcation typically at C3-C4 level
• Divides into ICA and ECA
• Carotid bulb at bifurcation - area of low resistance flow

sections.title: Internal Carotid Artery (ICA)
sections.content:
Supplies the brain:

• Larger diameter than ECA
• Posterolateral position
• NO extracranial branches
• Low resistance waveform (continuous diastolic flow)
• Enters skull through carotid canal

sections.title: External Carotid Artery (ECA)
sections.content:
Supplies face and scalp:

• Smaller diameter than ICA
• Anteromedial position
• Multiple branches:
  - Superior thyroid (first branch)
  - Lingual
  - Facial
  - Occipital
  - Posterior auricular
  - Maxillary
  - Superficial temporal
• High resistance waveform (less diastolic flow)

sections.title: Distinguishing ICA from ECA
sections.content:
How to tell them apart:

1. Branches: ECA has them, ICA doesn't
2. Size: ICA is larger
3. Position: ICA is posterolateral
4. Waveform: ICA is low resistance
5. Temporal tap test: Oscillations appear in ECA

sections.title: Circle of Willis
sections.content:
Provides collateral circulation:

• Connects both ICAs and vertebrobasilar system
• Allows blood flow to brain even if one vessel is occluded
• Anterior circulation: ICAs
• Posterior circulation: Vertebral arteries → Basilar artery
• Complete in only ~50% of people

keyTakeaways: CCA has no branches before bifurcation
ICA has no extracranial branches (key identifier)
ECA is smaller, anteromedial, with multiple branches
ICA = low resistance, ECA = high resistance

categories.title: Hemodynamics & Doppler
categories.description: Understand blood flow dynamics and Doppler waveform interpretation

topics.title: Doppler Waveform Analysis
topics.quickSummary: Arterial waveforms range from triphasic (normal) to monophasic (abnormal). Venous waveforms should be phasic with respiration and augment with compression.
clinicalPearls: Loss of triphasic = proximal disease or increased resistance
Monophasic waveform = significant proximal stenosis or occlusion
Pulsatile venous flow in legs = right heart failure or TR
Non-phasic venous flow = proximal obstruction (think DVT)

sections.title: Arterial Waveforms
sections.content:
Normal arterial flow has three phases:

Triphasic Waveform (Normal):
• Phase 1: Forward flow in systole (sharp upstroke)
• Phase 2: Brief reverse flow in early diastole
• Phase 3: Small forward flow in late diastole
• Indicates: Normal vessel, no proximal stenosis
• High resistance flow pattern

Biphasic Waveform:
• Forward systolic flow
• Reverse diastolic flow (no third phase)
• May be normal variant OR mild disease
• Common in older patients

Monophasic Waveform (Abnormal):
• Forward flow only
• No reverse component
• Rounded, dampened appearance
• Indicates: Proximal stenosis/occlusion OR high resistance state
• Distal to significant stenosis

sections.title: Venous Waveforms
sections.content:
Venous flow characteristics:

Phasic Flow (Normal):
• Flow varies with respiration
• Increases with expiration
• Decreases with inspiration
• Normal in peripheral veins
• Indicates patent vein to heart

Pulsatile Flow:
• Flow varies with cardiac cycle
• Normal: Near heart (IVC, iliac veins)
• Abnormal: In leg veins
• Suggests: CHF, tricuspid regurgitation, RV dysfunction

Continuous/Non-phasic Flow (Abnormal):
• Constant flow, no respiratory variation
• Indicates proximal obstruction
• Common finding with DVT
• May see collateral vessels

sections.title: Waveform Analysis Tips
sections.content:
What waveforms tell you:

• Sharp upstroke = good proximal flow
• Rounded upstroke = proximal stenosis
• High peak = stenosis at sample site
• Loss of reverse flow = distal disease or low resistance
• Dampened waveform = proximal occlusion
• Aliasing on color = high velocity (stenosis)

keyTakeaways: Triphasic = normal, monophasic = abnormal (arterial)
Loss of phasicity in veins = proximal obstruction
Pulsatile leg veins = cardiac problem
Waveform shape reveals proximal and distal disease

topics.title: Spectral Doppler Optimization
topics.quickSummary: Proper sample gate placement, angle correction, and gain settings are essential for accurate velocity measurements and waveform interpretation.
clinicalPearls: Doppler angle must be <60° for accurate velocities
Sample gate should be 1/2 to 2/3 vessel diameter
Keep sample gate centered in vessel
Wall filter too high = lose low velocity information

sections.title: Sample Gate Placement
sections.content:
Proper gate placement is critical:

✓ Good Sample Gate:
• Size: 1/2 to 2/3 vessel diameter
• Position: Centered in vessel lumen
• Length: Covers area of interest
• Not touching vessel walls

✗ Poor Sample Gate:
• Too large: Spectral broadening artifact
• Off-center: Inaccurate velocities
• Too small: May miss peak velocities
• At vessel wall: Includes low velocity boundary layer

sections.title: Doppler Angle
sections.content:
Angle correction for accurate measurements:

• Optimal angle: 45-60°
• Must be <60° for accuracy
• Angle too steep (>60°): Error increases exponentially
• 0° angle (perpendicular): No Doppler shift detected
• Align angle cursor parallel to vessel walls
• In stenosis: Align with direction of flow

sections.title: Spectral Broadening
sections.content:
Understanding the spectral window:

Normal Spectral Window:
• Clear area beneath systolic peak
• Indicates laminar flow
• Uniform RBC velocities

Spectral Broadening (Filling of Window):
• Turbulent flow pattern
• Range of RBC velocities

Causes:
1. Pathologic:
   • Stenosis
   • Post-stenotic turbulence
   • Disturbed flow

2. Technical:
   • Sample gate too large
   • High gain settings
   • Improper angle

sections.title: Optimization Settings
sections.content:
Key Doppler controls:

Gain:
• Adjust to fill spectrum without excessive noise
• Too low: Lose weak signals
• Too high: Noise, artifactual broadening

Wall Filter:
• Removes low-frequency motion (vessel wall)
• Too high: Lose low velocity flow
• Too low: Wall motion artifact
• Typical: 50-100 Hz

Scale/PRF:
• Adjust to prevent aliasing
• Too low: Aliasing artifact
• Too high: Compressed waveform, lose detail

Sweep Speed:
• Controls horizontal display
• Faster: More detail, fewer cardiac cycles
• Slower: More cycles, less detail

keyTakeaways: Sample gate = 1/2 to 2/3 vessel diameter, centered
Doppler angle must be <60° (45-60° optimal)
Clear spectral window = laminar flow
Spectral broadening = turbulence OR technical error

categories.title: Vascular Pathology
categories.description: Recognize and characterize vascular diseases and abnormalities

topics.title: Atherosclerotic Plaque & Stenosis
topics.quickSummary: Atherosclerosis causes arterial narrowing through plaque buildup. Stenosis severity is graded using velocity ratios and waveform analysis.
clinicalPearls: PSV ratio >2.0 = ≥50% stenosis (peripheral arteries)
Plaque composition matters: Hypoechoic = lipid-rich, echogenic = calcified
Always measure pre-stenotic, at stenosis, and post-stenotic
Collateral vessels indicate chronic occlusion

sections.title: Plaque Characteristics
sections.content:
Understanding plaque appearance:

Plaque Echogenicity:
• Hypoechoic (dark): Lipid-rich, hemorrhage
• Isoechoic (gray): Fibrous tissue
• Hyperechoic (bright): Calcification, fibrosis
• Heterogeneous: Mixed composition

Plaque Surface:
• Smooth: More stable
• Irregular: Higher embolic risk
• Ulcerated: Highest risk
• Surface defect visible

Plaque Texture:
• Homogeneous: Uniform appearance
• Heterogeneous: Variable composition
• Calcified: Acoustic shadow
• Soft: More likely to embolize

sections.title: Stenosis Grading
sections.content:
Quantifying arterial narrowing:

Carotid ICA Stenosis (NASCET Criteria):
• Normal: PSV <125 cm/s
• <50%: PSV <125 cm/s (with plaque)
• 50-69%: PSV 125-230 cm/s, Ratio <4.0
• 70-99%: PSV >230 cm/s, Ratio >4.0
• Near occlusion: String sign, very low flow
• Occlusion: No flow

Peripheral Artery Stenosis:
• <50%: Velocity ratio <2.0
• 50-75%: Ratio 2.0-4.0
• >75%: Ratio >4.0
• Critical: Monophasic, dampened waveform

sections.title: Stenosis Hemodynamics
sections.content:
What happens at stenosis:

At Stenosis:
• ↑ Velocity (narrowing → acceleration)
• Turbulent flow
• Spectral broadening
• Aliasing on color Doppler
• Post-stenotic turbulence

Proximal to Stenosis:
• Normal or slightly dampened waveform
• May see prestenotic dilation

Distal to Stenosis:
• Dampened waveform
• Loss of triphasic pattern
• Delayed systolic upstroke
• Decreased velocities

With Occlusion:
• No flow at occlusion site
• Dampened monophasic flow distally
• Collateral vessels visible

keyTakeaways: Higher PSV and velocity ratios = more severe stenosis
Waveform changes occur proximal, at, and distal to stenosis
Plaque composition affects stability and embolic risk
Always correlate velocity with waveform and B-mode findings
